# How This Book Is Written {.unnumbered}

A book about AI-native design systems should be candid about how it was itself produced. I am writing this synthesis during an academic sabbatical at Harvard University while spending dedicated time at ETH Zürich, with the goal of bringing a fully polished volume to completion by the end of 2027. Releasing early drafts in the open creates a real form of personal accountability, while working with generative AI systems every day exposes both their practical utility and their failure modes.

Because computer architecture, machine learning, and electronic design automation have historically operated as separate communities with their own physical constraints, vocabularies, and evidence standards, bringing them into a single discipline required an explicit authoring workflow. To connect these domains with engineering precision, I developed an AI-assisted authoring engine grounded in backward-design principles adapted from [Harvard's Learning Incubator (LInc)](https://linc.seas.harvard.edu/). This monograph is about AI-native design systems, in which learned methods are built into the design loop itself, whereas writing it is AI-assisted work inside a workflow I direct, in which coordinated agents draft text, write analysis and figure code, collect data, and audit results. Although I have found generative models adept at retrieving broad interdisciplinary literature and surfacing cross-domain connections, raw information retrieval lacks physical intuition, architectural taste, and domain-specific verification. To supply that missing rigor, I structured the authoring workflow around specialized, simulated review roles: learner panels evaluate pedagogical clarity, senior architect panels test technical bounds, systems panels inspect tool interfaces, and citation auditors check citations against their sources. These review roles report into the workflow I direct, and accepted work then passes through an automated validation harness that compiles the manuscript and verifies formatting (@fig-author-ai-workflow).

![**The authoring workflow keeps commit authority with the author.** Backward design establishes intent first. Generation roles propose drafts, and the diagram draws the orchestration that routes those drafts between roles as an inter-agent system bus, an on-chip analogy rather than a literal component. Simulated review panels supply critique. The author at the central hub holds commit authority over what reaches the deterministic validation harness, much as a reorder buffer decides which speculative results retire.](images/fig-author-ai-workflow){#fig-author-ai-workflow width="100%" fig-alt="Architecture diagram showing Stage 1 Backward Design, Stage 2 Human-in-the-Loop Core and Simulated Agent Review Panels, Stage 3 Validation Harness."}

That human commit step shows quickly why generation speed is not synthesis quality. In one early draft, a set of generation agents produced many pages of fluent prose on hardware–software co-design within minutes; on close inspection, however, the text blurred the boundary between cycle-accurate simulation and physical signoff checks, substituting smooth generalities for hard engineering trade-offs. I discarded the draft and rebuilt the section from the underlying trade-offs. Generative models propose candidate structures, but I set the rules they work under and hold commit authority over what enters the book, although some mechanical and rule-driven passes run without my reviewing every line. That division of responsibility applies to automated system and chip design just as it does to monograph synthesis. Whether evaluating an AI-generated bus topology or an AI-generated chapter draft, an architect must decide which distinctions matter, what the evidence supports, where an analogy breaks down, and what must be excised.

Editorial judgment also has to be tested against executable reality, which is why the manuscript is developed alongside runnable reference implementations. While the book's content and code samples are freely readable online, the engineering value of an AI-assisted authoring engine lies in how its governance, deterministic test harnesses, and multi-agent review panels are structured to catch fabrication, and those checks have limits. The validation harness checks form rather than truth, and the review panels are models that can share the blind spots of the models they review. A citation auditor, for example, is tasked with flagging a reference whose source does not say what the sentence claims, so that the claim can be corrected or cut. Just as an engineering organization guards its internal verification methodology, the rigor of this synthesis depends on my holding commit authority over what enters the book and answering for it.

An open draft invites readers to serve as one more check on its clarity. Writing is how I test whether I understand a subject deeply enough to teach it, and an explanation that cannot survive a reader's scrutiny is incomplete. I welcome your critique and value your feedback. If you spot a flaw, an imprecise claim, or a trade-off that requires a harder test, please reach out to me directly.
